title: Read the Constraints, Pick the Complexity

scenes.say: Count the pairs in two hundred thousand numbers that add to zero. One program runs two hundred seconds and fails. Another finishes instantly. By the end, you'll read the limits and know which one to write.

lines.text: Count pairs that add to zero
Read the limits. Pick the right one.

scenes.say: Today's plan. First, the one second budget. Then the cheat sheet that turns n into a complexity. Then we count pairs two ways, slow and fast.

scenes.title: Will it finish in one second?
scenes.statement: The judge gives you one second and tells you n. Decide which algorithms can possibly pass.
scenes.say: One second, then the judge kills your program. Which algorithms survive? Say n is two hundred thousand. The survivors: n log n or better. Roughly a hundred million steps fit in that second.
scenes.note: budget: about 10⁸ simple steps per second

scenes.head: A wallet of 100 million steps
scenes.say: Your gain: know in ten seconds which ideas are worth typing. The judge allows about one hundred million simple steps per second. That's your wallet. Every algorithm has a price, in steps. Price above the wallet? Time limit exceeded.

scenes.head: Worked example: n = 200,000
scenes.say: Say n is two hundred thousand, against a budget of one hundred million. N squared needs forty billion steps, four hundred times too many. Too slow. N log n is n times about eighteen: three and a half million. Easy. Plain n needs two hundred thousand. The limit says: n log n or better.
Pause and predict. A hundred thousand items, a one second limit. Which of these fits?
scenes.q: n = 100,000 and a 1-second limit. What fits?

scenes.head: Steps for n = 100,000
scenes.say: Answer: O of n and n log n fit. Plain n is a hundred thousand steps. N log n is under two million. N squared needs ten billion. At a hundred million a second, that's a hundred seconds.

scenes.title: Which complexity does this n allow?
scenes.statement: Every problem hides a hint in its limit on n. Read it, then name the complexity you can afford.
scenes.say: Every limit on n is a hint. A million? Then n log n, or plain n, is expected. Read any n that way, before you write one line of code.

cues.output: n log n, or plain n

scenes.head: The setter leaves you a hint
scenes.say: Most candidates spot two loops and start typing. Then the setter's trap springs. He wrote his own solution, timed it, and set n just under its limit. So n is a hint about the answer.

scenes.head: Cheat sheet: small n
scenes.say: The cheat sheet. Around ten, try every order: ten factorial is under four million. Around twenty, try every subset: two to the twentieth is about a million. Around five hundred, three nested loops, right at the edge.

scenes.head: Cheat sheet: big n
scenes.say: Keep going. Around five thousand, n squared: two nested loops. A million needs n log n, or plain n. A hundred million needs plain n, with a small constant. And ten to the eighteen? Only log n, or a formula.
Your turn. A problem says n is at most three thousand. Which is the biggest complexity that still fits? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: One more loop, out of budget
scenes.say: O of n squared. Three thousand squared is nine million, comfortable. Cubed is twenty seven billion, hopeless. Same n, one more loop, and you leave the budget behind.

scenes.title: Count pairs that add to zero
scenes.statement: Given n numbers, count the pairs of positions whose values add to zero.
scenes.say: Two hundred thousand numbers, and you must count the pairs that add to zero. Take two, minus two, five, minus two, two. Four pairs. Doing it by trying every pair is too slow.
scenes.note: n up to 200,000: brute force is too slow

scenes.head: Count pairs that add to zero
scenes.say: Walk left to right, with a notebook of numbers seen so far. Two comes first. Has minus two come before? No. Write two down. Next, minus two. Has a two come before? Once. Count one. Note it too. Five has no partner. File the five. Minus two again. A two came once. Count two. Note it again. Last, two. Minus two came twice. Count four.

scenes.head: Brute force: two loops
scenes.say: The brute force is two loops. It checks each pair once: twenty billion checks when n is two hundred thousand. That's still two hundred times the budget.

panels.label: too slow

scenes.head: The fix: remember what you saw
scenes.say: The fix: remember. The notebook is a hash map: each lookup takes one step. For each x, it already knows how many minus x came before. Add that to the count, then write x down. One pass, O of n. On our array, it prints four.

scenes.head: n = 200,000: two prices
scenes.say: Steps for our pair counting problem, two ways. The brute force needs twenty billion checks, about two hundred seconds. The map needs two hundred thousand lookups. That's the whole lesson: the limit chose the algorithm.
Your turn. Add one more minus two at the end of the array. What does fast print now? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: The new minus two
scenes.say: Six. The new minus two meets every earlier two. There are two of them, at positions zero and four. Four plus two is six.

scenes.head: What the table leaves out
scenes.say: What the table leaves out. A two second limit? Budget doubles, about two hundred million steps. Does n log n always pass? Not with a big constant, like maps. Memory? A million ints is four megabytes. Common mistake: brute force before reading n.
rows: Does n log n always pass?
not with a big constant, like maps

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What can you afford? About a hundred million steps a second. N of two hundred thousand? N log n or better. Brute force? Forty billion steps, two hundred seconds.

scenes.head: Cheat sheet, one row each
scenes.say: Cheat sheet, one row each. Ten: n factorial, try every order. Twenty: two to the n, try every subset. Five hundred: n cubed. Five thousand: n squared. A million: n log n, or plain n.

scenes.head: Follow-up: 100,000 items
scenes.say: Three thousand items, n squared? Nine million steps, easy. A hundred thousand, n squared? Ten billion, too slow. Then n log n: about 1.7 million, fine.

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode one, Two Sum: n is ten thousand, so even n squared passes. LeetCode fifteen, Three Sum: n is three thousand, so aim for n squared. LeetCode two thirty nine, Sliding Window Maximum: a hundred thousand, so brute force fails.
rows: n ≤ 10⁴: O(n²) passes, O(n) is cleaner

scenes.say: So say this. The judge gives about a hundred million steps. Read n first, then match the complexity. Two hundred thousand needs n log n or better.

n = 200,000 needs O(n log n) or better.
